title: Dipa Ma
hook: the Indian laywoman who lost her family, found peace through meditation, and taught many

segments.voice: Yesterday, women walking back into the ordination hall. Your line: taking the old story at its word. Did you find a nun's name, and one thing she said? Day one thousand eighteen.

A small woman in a white sari sits in a cramped apartment in Calcutta. Her visitors are students, neighbors, sometimes Westerners who have traveled a long way. She isn't a nun. She has no temple. She cooks, she looks after her grandson, and she teaches meditation from the floor of her home. Years earlier, people who knew her say, grief had left her so weak she could barely climb the steps of a temple. Today is the story of how she got from there to here.
screen: `A WHITE SARI, A SMALL APARTMENT.` → `NO TEMPLE, NO ROBES.` → `ONCE TOO WEAK TO CLIMB THE STEPS.`

segments.voice: Her name was Nani Bala Barua, and people came to call her Dipa Ma, mother of Dipa, after her daughter. She grew up in a Buddhist family in Bengal, married, and moved with her husband to Burma. Then the losses came, one after another, as her students tell it: children who died, and then her husband. She was left with her young daughter Dipa, with grief, and with a body that was failing. A doctor, the story goes, told her that her real illness was sorrow, and that she should learn to meditate. So she went to a meditation center in Rangoon. The early days were hard. Her students tell how, on her way to the center, she would stop and stop, and finally crawl up the stairs. But she kept going. She practiced with the method of noting, naming each movement of body and mind as it happened, and over time, her students say, the grief loosened its hold and her health came back. Later she moved to Calcutta and taught there, mostly to householders like herself: mothers, workers, people who couldn't leave for a monastery. Some of the teachers who later brought insight meditation to the West studied with her. What she told them was plain. Practice in the kitchen. Practice while you cook, while you wash, while you look after a child. You don't need a cave. The thing worth remembering is the order of the story. She didn't heal first and then practice. She practiced while she was broken, and rebuilt from there, one noted step at a time.
screen: `NANI BALA BARUA, CALLED DIPA MA.` · `LOSS AFTER LOSS, THEN ILLNESS.` · `CRAWLING UP THE STAIRS TO PRACTICE.` · `TEACHING HOUSEHOLDERS IN CALCUTTA.` · then, large: `PRACTICE IN THE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like it: honor someone who rebuilt. Sit, and let the breath come and go. Bring to mind a person you know who went through something hard and slowly put a life back together. A grandparent, a friend, a neighbor, maybe you. Don't tell the whole story to yourself. Just picture them on an ordinary day afterward: making breakfast, going to work, laughing at something small. Let the respect be quiet. If your mind drifts, note it, wandering, and come back to their face. The bell holds the time.
Dipa Ma. A laywoman who practiced through grief, rebuilt her life, and taught householders to meditate right where they lived. Today's word.
Your line: she rebuilt. Today, while you do one chore, washing up, folding, cooking, give it your full attention the way Dipa Ma taught. Day one thousand eighteen.

howItsDone: Insight meditation teachers often tell Dipa Ma's story as an example of a householder's practice, and some retreat centers and sitting groups encourage people to bring noting into chores, cooking and caring for family.

fork.setup: you're Dipa Ma, so weak with grief you can hardly climb the stairs to the meditation hall. what do you do?
options: wait at home until you're stronger
crawl up the stairs and practice

fork.reveal: her students say she crawled up the steps and kept practicing, and the healing came through the practice, not before it.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation teachers are monks who live far away.
what it means: Dipa Ma was a grieving laywoman who rebuilt through practice and taught householders at home.
what a scholar hears: a figure in the Burmese noting lineage whose students carried insight meditation to the West.

sources.ref: Accounts of Dipa Ma's life by her students (e.g. Amy Schmidt, Dipa Ma: The Life and Legacy of a Buddhist Master)

notes: No public-domain source; all biographical details paraphrased from student accounts and framed as 'her students say' / 'the story goes'. Confirm: born Nani Bala Barua in Bengal (Chittagong area, now Bangladesh), moved to Burma after marriage, loss of children and husband, the doctor's advice, practice in Rangoon (Mahasi center / with Munindra), crawling up the stairs, later teaching in Calcutta.
Name 'Dipa Ma' glossed as 'mother of Dipa', after her daughter; standard but confirm.
'Some of the teachers who later brought insight meditation to the West studied with her' left unnamed on purpose (commonly Joseph Goldstein, Sharon Salzberg, Jack Kornfield). Confirm.
The index calls her 'the Indian laywoman'; she was Bengali-born, lived long in Burma and later in Calcutta. Script avoids the label; consider an index note.
Noting method links back to day 1011 (Mahasi); angle here is grief and householder practice.
Editor pass: cut the age claim "married young" (not in a cited text); rest checked and kept.
